One-line judgment: clinical neuropsychologists do not simply 'give someone a psychological test'; they apply neuropsychological theory and standardized tests to assess higher brain function and behavioral problems related to acquired or developmental neurological disease, and are accountable for test validity, result interpretation, and report boundaries. O*NET defines this occupation as 'assessing and diagnosing patients with neurobehavioral problems caused by acquired or developmental diseases of the nervous system and recommending treatment, such as therapy, medication, or surgery, after diagnosis', and this page follows the exact occupation of O*NET-SOC 19-3039.03.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to align interviews, standardized tests, record review, and collateral information item by item for one question, and can accept long hours of sitting, reading, and writing while staying cautious on high-stakes judgments; O*NET work context shows 100% work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting every day, 92% use email every day, 91% hold face-to-face discussions every day, 83% have a great deal of freedom in making decisions, 88% work more than 40 hours in a typical week, 71% sit continually or almost continually, 67% consider precision or accuracy extremely important, and 42% feel time pressure every day.

Conditions for pausing before heavy investment: you have not yet walked through a complete assessment loop from referral and administration to validity checking and report and feedback, and have not checked test norms, language and cultural background, and the qualification boundaries of diagnosis and prescribing; the preparation level for this occupation is Job Zone Five (extensive preparation needed), with an SVP range of 8.0 and above, and the education distribution on the page shows 92% of respondents answering that postdoctoral training is required and 8% answering that a doctoral degree is required (the page shows only these two tiers); the occupation page does not mark this code as Bright Outlook, and this page does not describe it as a high-growth occupation.

Education, training, specialty certification, licensure, and job authorization must each be checked separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Five (extensive preparation needed), with an SVP range of 8.0 and above; the common U.S. path is doctoral training in psychology, a clinical internship, specialized postdoctoral training in neuropsychology, and state psychologist licensure, and ABCN specialty certification additionally requires a materials review and examinations but does not replace state licensure; in the Chinese mainland you should first verify the medical institution where the position sits, the professional technical qualification, and the specific authorization, and must not claim, on the basis of an overseas Clinical Neuropsychologist title alone, that you can diagnose independently, prescribe, or provide psychotherapy outside an institution; this page describes tasks and boundaries based on O*NET and public sources, and does not write a degree or training as a legal qualification.

Clinical neuropsychologists' work falls into three connected but independent work surfaces. The first is assessment and diagnosis: interviewing patients to obtain a complete history, administering neuropsychological assessments of intelligence, academic ability, attention, concentration, sensorimotor function, language, learning, and memory, distinguishing psychogenic from neurogenic syndromes and two or more suspected causes of brain dysfunction, and diagnosing and treating diseases involving central nervous system damage (such as cerebrovascular accidents, tumors, infectious or inflammatory diseases, degenerative diseases, traumatic brain injury, demyelinating diseases, and various dementing diseases). The second is reporting and result interpretation: writing or preparing detailed clinical neuropsychology reports based on data from psychological or neuropsychological tests, self-report measures, rating scales, direct observation, or interviews, establishing a neurobehavioral baseline to monitor progressive encephalopathy or recovery, and comparing patients' progress before and after medication, surgery, or behavioral intervention. The third is consultation, education, and supervision: consulting with other professionals about patients' neurological status, providing education or counseling to individuals and families, giving patients and their families feedback on assessment results and recommendations, designing or implementing rehabilitation plans for patients with cognitive impairment, educating and supervising interns, psychology trainees, or hospital staff, and continually reading the literature, exchanging views with peers, and participating in professional organizations or conferences to keep up with developments in neuropsychology.
Apply neuropsychological theory and standardized tests to assess higher brain function and behavior in support of diagnosis and treatment recommendations and rehabilitation decisions

Six recurring occupational judgments: whether the referral question and assessment scope are clear; whether history and cultural and language background are verified; whether administration follows standards with complete recorded conditions; whether validity and norm fit are checked; whether multi-source evidence agrees and the limits are written out; and whether the conclusions and recommendations remain within your own qualifications and authorization.
Judgment one: whether the referral question and assessment scope are clear

Before administering tests, write clearly 'what question is to be answered, which tests are needed, and what decision the conclusion will be used for', and for questions beyond the assessment scope or that neuropsychological tests cannot answer, state that clearly and hand them to the appropriate role.
Judgment two: whether history and cultural and language background are verified

Verify prior history, medication, educational history, and language and cultural background, because these factors affect test performance and norm fit, and ignoring them will misread background differences as functional deficits.
Judgment three: whether administration follows standards and records conditions completely

Administer tests under the conditions specified in the test manual and record the setting, duration, assistance, and deviations, so that the results can be reviewed by others rather than producing scores first and adding explanations later.
Judgment four: whether validity and norm fit are checked

Check validity indicators and the consistency of performance, judge whether the norms apply to this examinee's age, education, language, and cultural background, and for cases that do not fit, state the limitations in the report rather than applying the scores directly.
Judgment five: whether multi-source evidence agrees and the limits are written out

Compare test results with observation, history, collateral information, and other examinations, and for conflicts explain the possibilities and the parts that cannot be determined, so that the report can answer 'what is supported and what is not'.
Judgment six: whether the conclusions remain within the scope of your qualifications and authorization

paragraphs: The six directions share some capabilities with this occupation: assessment interviewing, standardized administration, result interpretation, report writing, and communication. The real differences lie in the object and the responsibility: neuropsychologists lean more toward research and assessment within the same assessment sequence, the clinical and counseling direction focuses on emotional and behavioral treatment, the psychiatry and neurology directions hold medical diagnostic and prescribing authority, the occupational therapy direction focuses on delivering functional training, and the physician assistant direction provides care support under supervision, while this occupation centers on the integrated assessment and reporting of brain-behavior relationships and is accountable for validity and interpretation boundaries. When choosing, it is better to first validate with one deliverable assessment report exercise rather than comparing names.

The basis for comparison is the task and work activity and work context descriptions on the O*NET-SOC 19-3039.03 page, the adjacent occupations and adjacent-occupation slug list registered in this evidence route, and the public occupational materials for each adjacent occupation; the comparison is an editorial compilation and does not constitute a conclusion about scope of practice or mutual recognition of qualifications.

The table below compares the positions and occupations adjacent to this one: neuropsychologists, clinical and counseling psychologists, psychiatrists, neurologists, occupational therapists, and physician assistants. The four columns answer the same set of questions: what this direction does, where the key difference from this occupation lies, and what kind of person is better suited to choose it.

Neuropsychologists and this occupation belong to the same neuropsychological assessment sequence, both assessing brain-behavior relationships with standardized tests; this occupation places more emphasis on combining with the clinical diagnosis of acquired or developmental neurological disease and may take part in treatment recommendations and consultation.

People willing to choose a role closer to clinical diagnosis and treatment recommendations within the neuropsychological assessment sequence suit this occupation; people who want research and assessment at the core suit the neuropsychologist direction.
Mainly neuropsychological assessment results, reports, and assessment data.
Neuropsychologists

Clinical and counseling psychologists focus on the assessment and psychotherapy of emotional and behavioral problems; this occupation centers on neuropsychological assessment and reporting for neurological disease and usually does not deliver psychotherapy as its main output.
People willing to do psychotherapy and psychological assessment suit that direction; people willing to do integrated brain-behavior assessment and write diagnostic reports suit this occupation.
Mainly psychotherapy and psychological assessment records and treatment plans.
Clinical and counseling psychologists

Psychiatrists hold medical diagnostic and prescribing authority and focus on medication treatment and medical management; this occupation focuses on neuropsychological assessment and reporting, and matters involving prescribing and medical diagnosis must be handed to the appropriate role.

People willing to study medicine and focus on medication and medical management suit that direction; people willing to do assessment and interpretation while accepting qualification boundaries suit this occupation.
Mainly diagnostic conclusions and prescriptions and course-of-illness records.
Psychiatrists

Neurologists focus on the medical diagnosis and treatment of neurological disease; this occupation assesses cognitive, emotional, and behavioral function in the context of neurological disease and produces assessment reports.
People willing to do neurological medical care suit that direction; people willing to use brain-behavior assessment to support diagnosis and rehabilitation decisions suit this occupation.
Mainly medical diagnosis and examinations and treatment plans.
Neurologists

Occupational therapists focus on functional training and rehabilitation of activities of daily living; this occupation provides assessment evidence and recommendations about cognitive and behavioral function and does not act as the main deliverer of daily functional training.

People willing to do functional training and rehabilitation delivery over the long term suit that direction; people willing to do assessment and reporting and to support rehabilitation plan design suit this occupation.
Mainly functional training records and rehabilitation plans.
Occupational therapists

Physician assistants provide care support and patient management under physician supervision; this occupation centers on neuropsychological assessment and reporting and usually does not carry out medical care and medication administration.
People willing to provide care support and patient management within a medical team suit that direction; people willing to do assessment and interpretation and write reports suit this occupation.
Mainly care support and patient management records.
Physician assistants

Moving from this occupation to an adjacent direction usually requires building new capabilities and qualifications: the neuropsychology direction requires further training in research and assessment methods; the clinical and counseling direction requires specialized training in psychotherapy and counseling; the psychiatry and neurology directions require medical education and licensure; the occupational therapy direction requires occupational therapy professional education and licensure; and the physician assistant direction requires physician assistant professional education and licensure. Assessment and reporting capabilities are transferable, but the qualifications and responsibilities and authorization scope of each direction must be re-obtained.

values: Fictional task: based on one fictional referral form and one set of fictional test and observation data, complete the assessment question definition and the validity verification and conclusion limit plan.

Fictional material: a fictional referral and history summary (including one missing prior examination and one language and cultural background note), a fictional test result and norm comparison table (including one abnormal validity indicator and one result inconsistent with the history), and fictional observation records.
Fictional condition: a fictional administration and scoring procedure (including validity indicators and norm use requirements).
Fictional constraint: a fictional feedback and referral requirement (including understandable expression and matters requiring referral).

Step one: write out the assessment question and the reasons for tool selection (list the questions that need answering and the tools chosen, and point out the missing prior material and the background note in the given material).

Step two: write out the validity verification and conclusion limit plan (explain the handling order for the abnormal validity indicator and the result inconsistent with the history, and which conclusions must not be written into the report before verification).

Step three: write a one-page feedback and referral summary (including the points to give the patient and family and the matters requiring referral and the documentation requirements) and explain which content requires confirmation by a person with the appropriate qualifications before it is issued.

entries.answer: Daily work centers on interviewing and standardized administration and evidence integration and reporting: interviewing patients to obtain a complete history, administering neuropsychological assessments of intelligence and attention and memory and language, distinguishing psychogenic from neurogenic presentations, establishing a neurobehavioral baseline and comparing progress before and after intervention, writing detailed clinical neuropsychology reports, consulting with other professionals about neurological status, and giving patients and families feedback on results and recommendations. O*NET work context shows 100% work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting every day, 91% hold face-to-face discussions every day, 67% consider precision or accuracy extremely important, and 88% work more than 40 hours a week.
entries.question: What do clinical neuropsychologists do every day?

entries.answer: Neuropsychologists and this occupation belong to the same neuropsychological assessment sequence; clinical and counseling psychologists focus on the assessment and psychotherapy of emotional and behavioral problems; psychiatrists and neurologists hold medical diagnostic and prescribing authority; occupational therapists focus on functional training and rehabilitation of activities of daily living; physician assistants practice under physician supervision; this occupation centers on the integrated assessment and reporting of brain-behavior relationships and is accountable for validity and interpretation boundaries. Shared capabilities do not mean the roles are interchangeable: the assessment object, reporting responsibility, and qualification requirements differ.
entries.question: Where is the boundary between this occupation and adjacent occupations?

entries.answer: That cannot be inferred. The core tasks of this occupation include judging test validity and norm fit, making differential judgments, integrating multi-source evidence into a conclusion, and giving feedback to patients and the referral team within time limits; tool output neither replaces those judgments nor removes confidentiality and test security and ethical obligations.
entries.question: Will AI replace clinical neuropsychologists?

entries.answer: The earlier-affected parts are those that can be structured and digitized: organizing and structuring interview records, scoring and norm lookup, report format drafts, and organizing result trends. The later-affected parts are those requiring judgment and accountability: test selection and validity judgment, differential and causal inference, conclusion limits and feedback, and judgments about qualification and authorization boundaries.
entries.question: Which tasks are most easily automated?

entries.answer: Selecting appropriate tests and judging validity and norm fit, deciding not to reach a conclusion when information is insufficient, giving complex results back to patients and families in an understandable way, and handling ethical and privacy and authorization boundaries. These capabilities depend on professional training and accountability.

description.text: Clinical neuropsychologists apply neuropsychological theory and standardized tests to assess brain-behavior relationships, centered on assessment and diagnosis, reporting and result interpretation, and consultation, education, and supervision: tasks and work context, the U.S. wage and BLS employment basis shown on the O*NET page (marked as the Psychologists, All Other combined-group basis), the Chinese mainland statistical basis and occupation-mapping gap, entry and qualification pathways, and the risks and practice, all in one view.

subject.name: Clinical neuropsychologists
subject.summary: Apply neuropsychological theory and standardized tests to assess higher brain function and behavioral problems related to acquired or developmental neurological disease: interview patients and obtain a complete history, administer assessments of intelligence and attention and memory and language, check validity and norm fit, integrate multi-source evidence into a report, establish a neurobehavioral baseline and compare progress before and after intervention, recommend treatment after diagnosis, give patients and families feedback on results and recommendations, and consult with other professionals about neurological status.
